title: Audi reveal new Formula 1 campus plans in Hinwil
excerpt:
Audi have revealed plans outlining a new campus for their Formula 1 operations in Switzerland, as the German manufacturer looks to increase their commitment to the sport.

Audi joined the F1 grid at the start of this season, taking over the Sauber outfit and their factory in Hinwil, and have released details of further expansion with the new campus set to be built less than one kilometre from the current base.

Elements of the new campus at Zurichstrasse have already become operational, doing so during the summer, with the full development set to be completed by 2030.

The team stated that "the existing site on Wildbachstrasse will remain fully operational and will subsequently be redeveloped as the team’s manufacturing centre and windtunnel operation.

"Formula 1 power units will continue to be developed and manufactured in Neuburg, Germany, while the team will retain its technical centre in Bicester, United Kingdom."

Audi currently sit eighth in the teams' standings, with hopes of moving up the grid in the coming years as further developments are made to their facilities.

“The campus will play an important role in helping us attract and retain world-class talent while providing the foundations required to achieve our long-term ambitions," said Team Principal Mattia Binotto.

“Building a successful Formula 1 team is ultimately about people. The best engineers, designers, mechanics and specialists want to work in an environment that allows them to collaborate, innovate and perform at their highest level. The campus will help us create exactly that environment.

“What makes this project particularly special is that it allows us to shape the future of Audi Revolut F1 Team from the ground up.

"Opportunities like this are rare in modern Formula 1. We are not simply moving into an existing facility; we are creating a home designed around our people, our culture and our ambitions. This campus is an important part of that journey.

“We are proud that the next chapter of Audi Revolut F1 Team will be written in Hinwil and I would like place on record my thanks to the Municipality of Hinwil itself.”

title: Drivers reflect on the key challenge they expect in Sepang
excerpt:
For half of the Formula 1 grid, Thursday was a first chance to take a proper look at a Sepang track that they’ve previously only seen on TV or experienced in factory simulators, and for the rest it was a chance to refamiliarise themselves with a venue that they last sampled nine years ago.

One thing came as no surprise to either track rookies or veterans though. Sepang has always been noted for a rough surface that gives tyres a hard time and, if anything, as the years have gone by it has become even more abrasive.

Managing tyre degradation will thus be a big story of the weekend for all, with two or three pit stops looking likely.

That’s good news for fans, for whom strategic variety can spice up races. It also makes life more interesting for the drivers, who generally not only enjoy the challenge of managing degradation but obviously want to seek a competitive advantage through car set-up or driving style.

“Maybe finally we see some deg because it's been a few weekends now in a row where there's been zero deg,” said Carlos Sainz. “And it makes the racing a bit less driver dependent. It's just about pushing flat out, and the car you have, you cannot manipulate the strategy or anything. So I wouldn't mind seeing a bit of deg.”

“I think it'll be high,” Oscar Piastri commented when asked about the subject. “It looks like sandpaper out there! So yeah, we'll wait and see. But I definitely think it's going to be challenging with tyre deg.

“Obviously I don't know how much racing or track running there's been recently and, anything that has been, the rain probably washes it off every afternoon anyway. I think it's going to be a pretty tough weekend, from every angle.”

World Championship leader Kimi Antonelli also anticipates that looking after tyres – in Qualifying and race trim – will be the big challenge.

“It's going to be completely different to what we had in these three races after the summer break because they were all new tarmac, no deg,” said the Mercedes driver. “Baku was a funny one, because the more you pushed, the better it was for the tyres, so this one is going to be completely different.

“I just did the track walk, and it's the roughest track tarmac that I've seen. Probably it’s similar to Bahrain in some places, maybe even more. So it might be a scenario where we see two, three stops in the race, also because it's so hot. So it's going to be interesting, but definitely very different driving, very different approach, because it's not only about long runs.

“It's going to be also about single lap, trying to extract the maximum grip over one lap, because tyres are not going be happy, especially when you come to Sector 3. They're going to be screaming quite a lot…

“It's going to be a new challenge, different to what we've been used to, and also practice I think you're going to have limited laps, especially when you try Quali simulation. So it's going to be important to be on top of it straight away.”

With its long straights, teams are expecting Sepang to provide lots of overtaking.

However, Antonelli’s team mate George Russell made an interesting observation on how the tyres might impact that.

“I think the big difference on this circuit compared to other so-called 'yo-yo' circuits is the tyre overheating,” he said. “Circuits such as Melbourne, Silverstone, Monza, there wasn't actually that much tyre overheating from the surface. Canada as well.

"That kind of allowed the drivers to stay a little bit closer, within that one second. Even in Baku it was quite cool, the drivers could stay close.

All the stories that got the Malaysia paddock talking

“Whereas here, surface overheating is going to be a huge thing. You'll be overheating the tyres even on the out lap of a Qualifying session, which may make it more challenging to follow closer and to re-attack once you've been overtaken. But that's a total unknown, currently.”

The other big talking point is the high likelihood of rain at some stage during the weekend, with a deluge on Wednesday afternoon providing the paddock with an early taste of what to expect.

Sepang is Round 16 of the World Championship, and yet we have still not seen a properly wet official session.

Many teams and drivers have little or no proper experience of running the 2026 cars in wet conditions, although some – notably Ferrari and Red Bull – have undertaken Pirelli testing.

“I've not driven in the wet in this car, so it is still a completely new experience for us,” said Lando Norris. “Obviously, things have improved a lot since the beginning of the year, which makes some of the concerns less. But it's still a new experience, so that's something we have to be ready for, and prepare for.”

It’s not just a question of tyres – it’s also about how to manage the PUs in the wet, and dealing with power delivery, especially in changeable conditions.

“It’s a good test for sure, if it rains,” said Sainz. “I think with all the issues we have with downshifts, with harvesting, power variability corner to corner, the wet is going to be a challenge for sure, both from a tyre standpoint – from what I heard, this year's wet tyre and inter tyre is quite a difficult tyre from people that have run it – plus the power unit factor. So it will be for sure a good test.”

You might think that, with the title in his sights, the last thing Antonelli needs is rain, given the potential lottery that it might create. However, he welcomes the chance to drive the W17 in wet conditions.

“It would be very interesting,” he noted. “On one side, it would be nice to do a few laps on the wet because to be fair, this year we've been so lucky with rain. We have avoided rain so many times, and we've been lucky for sure.

“I think it would be time to just do some laps in the rain, even in practice, just to see how it feels, how the tyre feels, how the power unit feels, how the car feels. Most of us have such little information on or experience on wets. So it will be interesting.”

Antonelli makes the intriguing point that the Sepang asphalt will actually be helpful in wet conditions, because the water drains away.

In addition, the rough surface – together with the high ambient – should help to address the temperature issues that drivers who have run the latest wets have highlighted.

“I think this track will be quite okay in the wet,” said Antonelli. “It always depends by how much it rains, because here it's very well known to be raining very much, and a good amount. But because the surface is so open, there's actually not a lot of standing water, unless it pours down.

“But if it rains normally, then it will be probably the best track to try these cars for the first time in the rain, because the tarmac is so open that the water just doesn't sit on top of the surface.

"It actually goes in-between the stones – so it makes less risk of aquaplaning and all this kind of stuff.”

title: Alonso staying at Aston Martin 'a strong signal' – Krack
excerpt:
Mike Krack believes that Fernando Alonso's decision to re-sign with Aston Martin for the 2027 season is "a strong signal to everybody", as the team looks to turn its fortunes around.

Ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia this weekend, Alonso confirmed he would remain with Aston Martin for next season after months of speculation about his future and whether he would retire.

While the Spaniard said his decision to continue in Formula 1 was due to a "fire inside", Alonso has also taken into account the trajectory of Aston Martin during a difficult season where it has occupied the back of the grid.

Speaking on Thursday's media day in Malaysia, Krack was pleased to retain the services of Alonso, as well as Lance Stroll.

“I think for me the fact that both drivers continue with us shows their trust and commitment in the team and its possibilities, and you don't have to have big words. I think the signature gives a good sign, a strong signal to everybody,” said Aston Martin's Chief Trackside Officer.

“I think we went through really tough times, especially at the beginning of the project, where we could almost not drive. And they were always positive. They are trying to encourage everyone, it's very positive in terms of leadership, and I think from that we can only progress further with having these two. But it is good motivation for everyone.

“For Fernando, it was also the question, does he want to continue? And I said many times, when you have someone with that track record, with that experience, you have to respect the request for time.

“I think it's not a secret that he's not so happy with the regulations. He wanted to see how that goes. So all-in-all, there have always been talks, and I think we are really happy that we came to the conclusion.”

Apart from Aston Martin's poor form, there was also the bigger picture question of how much Alonso enjoys racing the current generation F1 cars, having driven under many different sets of regulations over the past quarter of a century.

As he made clear in Sepang, Alonso sees a potential move to a 60:40 split of V6 and electrical power as a positive step that influenced his thinking, and as such his decision to commit can be seen as a thumbs-up for the direction that the rules are taking.

ANALYSIS: Why Alonso is staying at Aston Martin – and what it means for the 2027 grid

“I think it's not a secret that he's not so happy with the regulations. He wanted to see how that goes. So all-in-all, there have always been talks, and I think we are really happy that we came to the conclusion," added Krack.

“I think for drivers to enjoy, you have to have a quick car, and for the teams, by the way, as well. Nobody likes to be at the back. The only reason we do this is to race, to compete, and try to win.

“So I think even if the regulations are not great for what he perceives – and we must not forget he comes from a time where it was really flat-out racing, which maybe other drivers did not come from that time – I think you have to factor these things in."

title: Inside the chaos of the F1 drivers’ pre-Sepang training camp
excerpt:
Ahead of this weekend’s 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, several members of the Formula 1 grid headed on a ‘boys’ holiday training camp’ to Langkawi, spending their time playing chess, karting, training and heading out on boats. Here’s everything we know about their fun few days away.

The Williams pairing of Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz were the first to let slip about the trip while speaking on the Fan Stage at the recent Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Albon initially hinted that several drivers would be taking a few days off together, although he originally suggested it would be between the races in Malaysia and Singapore.

“We’re going to go on like a boys’ trip, I guess,” Albon said on the Fan Stage. “I think there are a few drivers where we’re going to hang out.”

“It’s going to be [a boys’ trip],” team mate Sainz then added. “We just realised no one’s bringing their girlfriend. But it’s not like we’re going to do anything exciting. We’re going to be in a resort in the middle of nowhere.”

Who attended the F1 boys’ trip?

The first glimpses of the drivers’ post-Baku getaway soon started appearing online, with locals sharing videos of them taking over a nearby karting track.

Joining Sainz and Albon were George Russell, Ollie Bearman, Oscar Piastri, Gabriel Bortoleto, and former F1 driver Roberto Merhi.

Sainz has since revealed that the trip came together almost spontaneously as several drivers tried to work out their travel plans from Azerbaijan to Malaysia.

“It was a combination,” he explained in Thursday’s print media session in Sepang, ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. “I think I saw that there were drivers trying to get on a flight to Malaysia from Baku on Saturday night, and rather than flying straight to Kuala Lumpur, I offered, ‘Why don’t we go somewhere else?’

“I found a hotel on an island to spend four or five days that looked really nice, with good cycling and a good gym. I said, ‘Why don’t we, instead of all flying to Kuala Lumpur for four days, which is more of a city and has less planned for us at least, fly to this nice resort?’

“We all jumped on that plane on Saturday night and flew straight from Baku to Langkawi. No one has probably ever flown from Baku to Langkawi. It’s the most random flight ever.”

Based in Langkawi, an archipelago off Malaysia’s northwest coast, the drivers made the most of their surroundings, heading out to see the sights while also using the opportunity to train ahead of the championship’s return to the Sepang International Circuit.

For Sainz, it also offered something that is surprisingly difficult to find during a Formula 1 season – proper time with the people he races against every weekend.

“Normally on race weekends, we never see each other,” he explained. “I never see all the guys that I got to spend time with because we all have our own commitments, so very rarely do you actually get to spend some proper time with them.

“The island we went to was quite fun because it was a small island and you put seven drivers on an island and see what they end up doing. It was a bit of a social experiment, for sure. Those four days, I would say, were interesting.

“I personally got to meet a lot more characters and some drivers that I didn’t know. I got to see their story, where they came from, how they ended up being the way they are, and why, and got to bond with them and understand them a bit better.

“For me, it was a very cool experience. I think we all left there quite happy with how it went.”

They also met up with reigning World Champion Lando Norris, who skipped the karting but was spotted unwinding with a game of chess on the beachfront. Is chess becoming the new padel?

Norris was quite happy to sit that particular activity out. “Everyone else went karting, but I did a bit of training and stayed in,” he said in Thursday’s print media session. “From what I heard, I certainly don’t think it made anyone treat each other any nicer. I think it made it even worse. From what I heard, everyone put each other in a wall at some point.”

Chaos at karting

That assessment might have been fair.

At the karting track, the drivers had to pick their own names and take photos for their profiles, which Russell later shared on social media.

The Mercedes driver raced under the pseudonym ‘G Dawg’, Albon opted for ‘Albino’, Sainz used his F1 race number ‘55’, while Piastri kept things simple with ‘OP’.

Speaking in Sepang, Russell explained exactly what unfolded once the F1 drivers were let loose on the circuit.

“It was wild,” the most recent F1 race winner stated. “Firstly I got helped out by the Malaysians... I went over to one of the guys like, ‘What is the best kart?’ and he put new tyres on, so I had this kart that was like 1.5 seconds quicker than everyone else and they were kicking off!

“It was carnage, but I thought it would be. Bortoleto ended up with bruises on his back, Piastri almost broke a rib, it was like a banger race! I actually pitted before the end because I was like, ‘I am going to break something here’, so I actually don’t know who won.

“Bearman put Merhi through a wall on the first lap of the race and then it was like, ‘Who else could hit someone else off the hardest?’”

Holiday or training camp?

While there was plenty of downtime, there was also some serious preparation going on ahead of two physically demanding races in Malaysia and Singapore.

“It was a good training camp, to be honest, and I’m working hard to prepare for this race,” Bearman said when asked about the trip during the pre-race press conference.

“You know, it’s a very unique climate that we have here and of course next week in Singapore as well.

“It was very fun to spend a bit of time with some of the guys outside of the circuit, and that’s also quite rare to be able to do that, and unlock a kind of a new side of all of the people that I was spending time with.

“I very much enjoyed myself, and it’s also nice to have a bit of a reset. A few days off, in a way, but also I’ve been training quite hard.”

Piastri echoed that sentiment, describing the trip as a rare opportunity for the drivers to switch off together away from the pressures of a race weekend.

“It was pretty last minute, but it was good fun being able to switch off from racing a bit,” he said. “It’s very rare that you get so many drivers actually spending time together away from a racetrack.

“At the end of the day, we’re 22 guys that love racing. Obviously, it’s a bit tricky to talk about certain things because we are racing each other, but we’ve got a lot in common that we just never really get to talk about. So it was quite nice.

“We all did our own separate things at points. It wasn’t like we were glued to each other the whole time. Maybe on the go-kart track we were! It was good fun, honestly.”

Can you still race your friends?

Spending several days on an island together might bring the drivers closer away from the circuit, but Norris does not believe that necessarily makes life any friendlier once the helmets go on.

“I think people are able to separate personal life and personal time from when you’re putting a helmet on,” he explained. “I think you become two different people. You are two different versions of yourself.

“So it’s nice that you get to spend a little bit of time with them outside of racing. I knew all of these guys pretty well already, but at the same time, they all went karting and I thought, ‘This is a bit of time when I don’t have to spend time with them.’ It’s nice to have a bit of time to myself and do my own thing. That’s what I enjoy a lot in my life.

“I don’t agree with that kind of statement that racing is more friendly. I think at times it’s the opposite of that. But it’s nice that we get to just be normal people away from the track, have a bit of downtime and get to see maybe a different side of people. That’s a good thing as well.”

Will we see more on Netflix’s Drive to Survive?

And there could also be considerably more footage from the trip still to come.

In one of the snaps shared in Russell’s Instagram photo dump, Norris could be seen with a camcorder for his recently announced Amazon Prime documentary.

However, just behind him stood several camera and boom-mic operators, reminiscent of the crews often seen filming Netflix’s Drive to Survive, as production continues on Season 9 of the popular show. Fingers crossed!

title: How Tom Cruise fell in love with Formula 1
excerpt:
Tom Cruise might be known by motorsport fans for portraying a racing driver in Days of Thunder, but did you know that he actually got behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car back in 2011? Ahead of the release of his latest movie Digger, here’s the story of that day, and how the Hollywood hero fell in love with Formula 1.

Cruise has always shown a great interest in the world of motor racing. During the late 1980s, the Hollywood hero actually gave professional racing a try thanks to his The Colour of Money co-star Paul Newman.

Cruise raced for the Newman/Sharp Racing team in sports cars, but quickly gained a reputation for his aggressive driving style and soon hung up his racing helmet. That didn’t stop him from enjoying racing through his movies, though, as well as keeping tabs on championships across both two and four wheels.

When Tom Cruise drove an F1 car

Cruise is no stranger to big stunts, fast machines and adrenaline rushes, but 15 years ago Red Bull Racing handed him the metaphorical keys to one of their Formula 1 cars.

Ahead of the inaugural United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of The Americas, Cruise had the chance to test one of their cars in a break from post-production of one of his Mission Impossible movies – showing his need for speed extended well beyond the big screen.

David Coulthard was on hand to offer advice, as a former Red Bull F1 driver and 13-time Grand Prix winner, with a 12-person crew from the team setting the car up correctly for Cruise and getting him ready for making history.

Taking place at the Willow Springs International Raceway in Southern California, Cruise and Coulthard did several passenger laps to familiarise themselves with the 4km circuit, before the movie star got suited up and ready to try it for himself in the 850-horsepower machine.

Cruise was instantly at home in the F1 car – despite never driving something like it before. The Golden Globe-winning actor banked 24 laps before coming into the pits to compare notes and telemetry, which resulted in him ultimately shaving 11 seconds off from his first to his last lap time.

There were a few off-track moments, but Cruise managed to keep the car running and bring it back to the pits. When he wasn’t on track, he was in the air with the Red Bull helicopter stunt team performing loops and daring manoeuvres.

Attending the F1 The Movie Premiere

It’s well known that Cruise supports the film industry. From taking photos at his local cinema watching the latest blockbuster or collaborating on movies through his production company, the man just loves motion pictures.

During the 2025 press tour for F1 The Movie, Cruise was pictured with his former Interview with the Vampire co-star Brad Pitt on the red carpet at the European premiere. F1 The Movie director Joseph Kosinski has previously worked closely with Cruise on flicks like Oblivion and Top Gun: Maverick.

Having shown his support on the red carpet, Cruise later took to Instagram to praise those behind F1's film debut, sharing a photo from the premiere with the caption: “Great night at the movies with my friends!! You guys crushed it!!”

Showing his support at Silverstone

Whether you know him as Tom Cruise, Ethan Hunt or “Maverick”, this Hollywood action hero has made several appearances at Formula 1 events over the seasons.

One of his most notable visits came on the weekend of his 60th birthday, when Cruise was papped under the 2022 British Grand Prix podium with Anthony Hamilton and Antonio Perez – fathers of Lewis and Sergio.

Cruise also pictured alongside Sir Jackie Stewart, standing next to Mercedes boss Toto Wolff in the garage mid-session, and even down for a chat on Martin Brundle’s grid walk. Cruise also spent time with Hamilton’s brother Nicolas ahead of the race - and was later snapped with Lewis himself after the race in a show of support.

Cruise had also been spotted at the 2021 British Grand Prix, as well as that year’s Goodwood Festival of Speed, where he chatted with 1978 Formula 1 World Champion and American racing legend Mario Andretti.

And Cruise was back at an F1 event when he visited the 2023 Miami Grand Prix – this time accompanied by Shakira. He even helped the Mercedes team with some pit stop practice!

As Digger lands in cinemas, it's fair to say Cruise has already created plenty of Formula 1 memories of his own. From life in the cockpit to behind-the-scenes access in the paddock, the star has spent more than a decade digging deeper into F1, and his passion for the sport remains clear to see.

title: Norris explains apology to Colapinto over Baku comments
excerpt:
Lando Norris has reflected on the apology he made to Franco Colapinto over his post-race comments at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, with the Briton conceding that he got “caught up in the heat of the moment” in Baku.

A lock-up from Colapinto at Turn 1 during the first Safety Car restart saw the Alpine driver run into team mate Pierre Gasly, which resulted in the Frenchman hitting the McLaren of Norris. The incident put both Gasly and Norris out of the race, while Colapinto limped to the pits but ultimately retired.

The Argentinian was subsequently handed a 10-second time penalty, which was converted into a five-place grid drop for this weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Speaking to the media immediately after the race, Norris stated that there were “some drivers that shouldn’t be in F1”, as well as suggesting that Colapinto should receive a ban. However, the World Champion later shared a statement on Monday via social media in which he explained that he had directly apologised to Colapinto for his comments.

Norris discussed this further during media day in Sepang, where he was quizzed on whether it was helpful to lean on other drivers as a support network when these scenarios occur.

“I've certainly leant on other drivers in the past for help in different situations and advice in different situations,” the 26-year-old said. “Not that I think this was necessarily that case at all – it was just me not saying the right things and saying some things that aren't a true reflection of me or what I really mean deep down.

“I think I don't normally get caught up in the heat of the moment but this was certainly one of the cases where I think I did, and for me the most important thing was to speak to Franco about it. He's the only guy, let's say, that I want to direct something to and care about in this situation, and that's what I did.

“I spoke to him already on Sunday night as soon as I could, and of course I put the post out later in the week to apologise, to let everyone know that I did it because there was also the rest of the world that I felt like I owed the apology to.

“As drivers we all get along, Franco is a good friend of mine who I get on well with. He always means well – he’s a very good guy. Of course, at the same time I felt like I owed him that apology more than everyone else.”

Alpine shared a statement condemning the “hate and abuse” posted online following the race in Azerbaijan, with Norris admitting that such behaviour is “not easy for anyone”.

“There's just a level of respect and humility that I think people should have,” he explained. “We all mistakes – one of those things was me making the mistake last weekend. There's a level of things, and as a community we need to understand how we can make it better.”

In terms of McLaren’s prospects at the Sepang International Circuit, Norris is hopeful that the venue might be better suited to the MCL40.

“I hope it's better than Baku – I expect it to be better than Baku,” the 13-time race winner said. “We certainly will be more confident if we can fix some of the problems I've had on my car. Over the weekend in Baku, it just made my car more tough than it needs to be, which is the straight-line speed and power problems we've been having.

“I want to believe so. I think we still believe as a team we have a competitive car and it's still strong in certain areas. Hopefully a combination of all these things means we can have a better weekend.”

title: Max Verstappen heads F1 rivals as Sepang makes return with soaring temperatures
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has ended the opening practice session from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on top of the timesheet.

F1 returned to Sepang for the first time in eight years as the circuit stands in as the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

As the most recent race winner around the circuit, Verstappen continued where he left off by pumping in the fastest time of the session, clocking a 1:37.520.

His effort placed him three-tenths of a second ahead of George Russell in the leading Mercedes.

[Article continues below]

The F1 drivers were subject to very hot conditions during the session, with the air temperature reaching 33°C during the 60-minute session.

It also caused the track temperature to peak at upwards of 58°C, causing strain for the tyres.

With Verstappen heading the field at the end of FP1 ahead of Russell, the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was third fastest - albeit almost eight-tenths down on his team-mate.

Charles Leclerc was the leading Ferrari driver in fourth, ahead of championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli enters the race weekend looking to protect his 66-point lead in the standings, having lost ground to Russell last time out in Baku.

Lewis Hamilton was sixth fastest in the second Ferrari, with the seven-time champion entering the weekend hoping to add to the sole victory he has at the event.

Pierre Gasly, whose F1 debut took place the last time F1 ventured to Sepang, was seventh for Alpine.

The Racing Bulls duo of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad were eighth and ninth respectively, while Nico Hulkenberg rounded out the top 10.

A number of engine-related grid penalties were confirmed during the session - including for Red Bull's Hadjar.

He will take a drop alongside Lindblad, whose significant engine overhaul will send him to the back of the grid on Sunday.

Franco Colapinto has also taken on a new engine to secure himself a grid drop that will be served alongside the penalty he carries over from Baku, when he caused a multi-car collision at a safety car restart.

title: Three drivers handed grid penalties for Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar, Arvid Lindblad and Franco Colapinto will all start Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang from down the order after taking grid penalties for exceeding their season's power unit component allocations.

Hadjar has fitted a seventh internal combustion engine of the campaign, one more than the five permitted under his pool, triggering a grid drop for the Red Bull driver.

Lindblad's situation is more severe.

The RB driver has taken a fifth ICE, exceeding his five-unit allowance, and has also introduced a fifth turbocharger and a fifth exhaust system, both beyond his four-unit limits in those categories.

The combined excess pushes Lindblad's penalty total past the 15-place threshold that forces a driver to the back of the grid regardless of further stacking, meaning the teenager will start Sunday's race from the rear.

Colapinto also arrives in Malaysia with a fifth ICE beyond his five-unit allocation, adding a further grid penalty on top of a separate sanction already applied to the Argentine.

The FIA stewards ruled Colapinto predominantly to blame for a lap-36 restart collision at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where he locked up into Turn 1, hit team-mate Pierre Gasly and triggered a chain reaction that also put Lando Norris into the wall, ending all three cars' races in Baku.

Because Colapinto retired before the original 10-second time penalty could be served, it was converted into a five-place grid penalty for Sepang, stacking with his engine-related drop.

title: Mercedes unveil huge array of F1 upgrades in final title push
excerpt:
Mercedes has unveiled its biggest upgrade package for over four months ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The W17s of F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli and George Russell possess a total of seven updated components as the team aims to cement its dominance this season over the final third of the campaign.

Antonelli heads into Sunday's race at the Sepang International Circuit with a 66-point lead over Russell. The nearest challenger from another team is Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who is 103 points adrift of the 20-year-old Italian.

In the constructors' championship, Mercedes holds a 160-point lead over Ferrari, with reigning champions McLaren a further 72 points adrift.

The cars this weekend are sporting a heavily modified floor, which includes modifications to the floorboard, the leading edge, corner and body.

The rest of the upgrades relate to the rear of the car, namely the suspension, as well as optimisation of brake drum winglets.

It is the most significant array of updates on the cars since the Canadian GP in May. Rivals Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all introduced major packages on their cars at a steady rate.

After the Dutch GP, team principal Toto Wolff stated that Mercedes did not have "the money to put developments on the car", and that it was "trying to evenly split" its upgrades through the season.

[Article continues below]

What have other F1 teams brought?

While Mercedes' rivals have not arrived in Malaysia empty-handed, their upgrades are minuscule in comparison.

McLaren has brought a new engine cover to facilitate the cooling demands of the Sepang track.

Red Bull has introduced a modified floor, while Ferrari has named a localised development around the diffuser winglet at the rear of the car.

In the midfield teams, Racing Bulls has made changes to both the front and rear wings, while Haas has updated its rear impact structure.

Finally, Alpine has trimmed the front brake drum exit to increase brake cooling around the track, with temperatures expected to consistently be over 30°C this weekend.

Williams, Aston Martin, Audi and Cadillac have all not listed any new parts for the race weekend.

title: Oscar Piastri raises menacing Mercedes concern: 'That's not a great sign'
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has highlighted a fresh worry about Mercedes after George Russell crushed the opposition in Baku and the W17 received a rare upgrade for the weekend in Malaysia.

Oscar Piastri has warned that the form Mercedes displayed in Baku, combined with a fresh upgrade package arriving at the Sepang International Circuit, points to a daunting weekend at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

George Russell took pole position for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by a staggering 0.837 seconds over nearest rival Charles Leclerc, with Piastri himself only a further thousandth back in third.

The Briton went on to win the race by just under two-tenths over Max Verstappen, with Piastri sliding to P14 after locking up at Turn 1 while battling the Red Bull driver for second place.

However, despite that narrow victory margin, the W17 was the class of the field, and Mercedes has now delivered its first major technical upgrade since May's Canadian Grand Prix.

The package is understood to be aimed at closing a deficit on conventional, downforce-sensitive circuits after recent struggles against McLaren, with some estimating a lap-time gain of around three tenths of a second.

Piastri, who lost out in a straight-line speed battle at Baku partly due to the MCL40's higher-drag, higher-downforce rear-wing configuration chosen to protect tyre temperatures in the slow corners, believes Sepang's flowing, high-speed layout should play into his car's hands.

"Hopefully it'll suit us a bit more than Baku did," Piastri told media, including RacingNews365. "Obviously, there's some pretty long straights here, but there's also some high-speed corners, which generally is where we've been strong this year.

"For me, on a personal level, I felt like I found a bit more understanding of what I need to do to get lap time out of the car.

"In the race, it was pretty clear that we were struggling a bit in terms of lap time compared to, especially, Mercedes and Red Bull."

Piastri unsure where McLaren sits

Sepang's layout stands in contrast to the tight, low-speed nature of Baku. The middle sector in particular is built around a sustained, high-speed sweeping sequence, most notably through the fast Turns 5 and 6 and the double-apex Turns 7 and 8, where cars need strong aerodynamic downforce and a stable platform to carry speed through the apex.

The circuit also demands that teams strike a balance, since it pairs those high-downforce sections with two long straights, meaning a car's aerodynamic efficiency matters just as much as outright cornering grip.

That combination is expected to suit McLaren's strengths this year far more than the stop-start demands of the Baku street circuit did, and explains Piastri's optimism heading into the weekend.

But the timing of Mercedes' upgrade adds another layer of intrigue. The revised bodywork and sidepod package has been designed to sharpen cornering performance without sacrificing straight-line speed.

With Russell having already demonstrated imperious one-lap pace in Baku, the prospect of Mercedes adding further performance at a circuit that should theoretically favour McLaren is clearly weighing on Piastri's mind.

"But I think here should suit us a bit more than Baku; where exactly will we sit? I don't know," the Australian added.

"Obviously, Mercedes is bringing upgrades, from what I hear. So, if they're on pole by eight tenths last week, that's not a great sign.

"So, let's wait and see. But I think it should suit us a bit better. And I think, for me, on a personal note, I felt happier in... maybe not happy, obviously, with the end result, but I feel like I had a bit more understanding."

title: George Russell responds to extreme theory over Mercedes F1 upgrade
excerpt:
Mercedes is unveiling a brand new upgrade package at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia this weekend.

George Russell has denied that Mercedes' upgrade package will offer a substantial burst in performance this weekend in Malaysia.

The W17 is being fitted with updates this weekend, marking just its second major enhancement of the 2026 campaign.

During the summer break, Mercedes technical director James Allison suggested Mercedes was finding "about half a second every two months" in the wind tunnel.

With Mercedes' last upgrade coming at the Canadian Grand Prix, that logic would suggest the Brackley-based squad could unleash up to one second in performance with its new parts.

When asked if it will be an upgrade to that scale, Russell told media including RacingNews365: "No. It's a good step, purely because it's been so long since we last brought an upgrade.

"So it's quite abnormal to have an upgrade back in May and then only again in October.

"As an individual upgrade step, it's large, but in a normal season, it's just sort of a normal trajectory that you would have expected from a May to an October upgrade package.

"I'm hoping it's going to propel us back to the front on these types of circuits, that have been more challenging for us in the past six races."

[Article continues below]

Driver

George Russell

British

63

Russell asserts 'nothing fundamental” changing with Mercedes' car

Early spy shots from the Sepang paddock show modifications to the sidepods, with changes also made to the underbody and the rear of the car.

The full list of upgrades will be announced in the build-up to the first practice session on Friday.

Outlining what Mercedes targeted from the upgrade package, Russell said: "The characteristics are changing.

"Nothing fundamental, just an increase in downforce is the main part of the package.

"We're pretty slippery in the straight, so on a drag perspective, it's been important for us to keep that sort of low drag, it's definitely helped us at a number of circuits.

"But it's just a pretty conventional upgrade package."

title: Liam Lawson baffled after Arvid Lindblad escaped Baku penalty
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has admitted his surprise that Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad did not receive a penalty for his role in the safety car restart crash at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Lawson's race ended when he was tipped around by Lindblad at the opening corner, with the incident also eliminating reigning champion Lando Norris.

Lindblad emerged unscathed from the collision and went on to score further points for the team, crossing the line in seventh place.

While Lawson was pleased to see the team add to its points tally, he was left surprised that Lindblad escaped unpunished.

“At the end of the day, from a team perspective, I'm obviously happy that we managed to score points out of that race,” he told media including RacingNews365.

“But in terms of the action in itself, I have absolutely no idea how it wasn't a penalty. I'm sure in another situation with another team or another driver, we probably push very hard [for a penalty].

“You can obviously appeal and stuff like this, that's something you can do. That's why I probably thought at the time, 'oh, maybe it wasn't that bad because there was no penalty'.

“Then after, I went and looked at the incident again, and I was pretty confused.”

[Article continues below]

Lawson has spoken to Lindblad

Lawson voiced his frustration over team radio at the time of the incident, having come out worse in one of the golden rules of racing.

When asked if he has spoken to Lindblad since the end of the race, Lawson said in Malaysia: “A little bit.

“To be perfectly honest, I had to leave very quickly after the race for a flight. Since then, we've spoken a little bit.

“Obviously, we come here and have to focus on this weekend and put that behind us. In terms of learnings from that incident again, it's something that was kind of outside my control.

“So I don't think those conversations need to be had with me.”

title: Kimi Antonelli makes eye-catching Mercedes F1 admission after 'conscious decision'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli does not believe that the Kimi of "12 months ago" would have been able to pull off his comeback drive in the Azerbaijan GP, after making a "conscious decision."

After clipping the Turn 1 wall during qualifying, Antonelli started 16th in Baku, his first major mistake since crashing in FP3 in the season-opening Australian GP in March.

During the race, he recovered to fifth place, earning 10 points, and limiting how far race-winner George Russell could eat into the 81-point deficit to the Italian. Antonelli arrives in Malaysia for the Bahrain GP 66 points clear of the Briton.

However, unlike the recent Italian GP where he stormed from 19th on the grid to equal the record for the second furthest back a driver has won a race from, Antonelli could not take the same risks in Baku, owing to the walls, which don't feature at Monza.

Reflecting on his personal growth from 2025, Antonelli described how 12 months ago, he would not have been capable of assessing the situation and deciding simply to bank the 10 points he was able to collect rather than risking more for a potential no-score.

"I don't think the Kimi of 12 months ago would have been capable [of the drive in Baku]," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think it was one of those weekends and one of those races where I had to accept that I couldn't drive on the limit because yes, I was driving under the limit, but it was a conscious decision that I made after the start of the race.

"Because I also felt I didn't feel so confident on pushing 100% the whole race. So I didn't want to make mistakes, so I just took this conscious decision, and it was one of those races where I had to be happy with a P5, because in this case, it could have been much worse.

"It could have been a DNF, but it was still a decent drive and good points that will always make the difference at the end of the season. But definitely, I feel, looking back at the race, I think it was much better than what I thought right after it because of the decision I took."

The article continues below.

Antonelli's decision

Explaining how he carried this out, Antonelli revealed the instruction he had told himself to ensure he did not suffer a first driver-related non-score of the year, with his Barcelona and Silverstone non-scores being car-related.

"I didn't really like driving under the limit. I felt a bit too slow, but the learning was that sometimes you have to accept these kinds of situations," he continued.

"You have to set to to settle for a result that even you know you didn't expect or you didn't want; you settle for a P5, and in the race, I learnt even more about myself, about how I think, how I react to certain things, and trust me, it was very hard to make that decision after I started the race to just sit back and take it.

"Baku was the first time where I actually had to tell to myself: 'Look, just take the least amount of risk as possible, and just take advantage of other people's mistakes and just bring it home.'

"Because in the end, it was such a disrupted weekend where everything was going wrong from FP1, missing 45 minutes in FP1, 35 minutes in FP2, and crashing in qualifying."

title: Max Verstappen signals greatest Red Bull desire as drought continues
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is still waiting for his first victory of the 2026 season.

Max Verstappen has highlighted his goal of chasing a first win of the 2026 season, despite a run of podium finishes that has kept Red Bull in the constructors' championship picture.

The four-time world champion finished second in Baku last time out, just 0.196 seconds behind race winner George Russell, but the result extended his winless run to 15 rounds.

Verstappen sits sixth in the drivers' standings on 163 points, some 139 behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with Mercedes having won 11 of the 15 races held so far.

Red Bull has slipped to fourth in the constructors' standings, behind Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren, as the Milton Keynes-based team has struggled to match the development pace of its rivals through 2026.

The Dutchman has nonetheless kept Red Bull competitive on raw pace in recent rounds, converting that into a string of podium finishes even as outright wins have eluded him.

"Unfortunately, we're not outscoring Mercedes. They are actually the fastest ones, or at least they were for most of the season," Verstappen told media including RacingNews365.

"I'm trying everything I can. We are scoring quite a few podiums now, but I want to win.

"That's what I'm here for and I'm getting close, but I want to at least win one race this year. So, I hope we can do it at some point, but we have some solid results."

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Verstappen cautious over Malaysia chances

Red Bull brought a revised floor, diffuser and sidepod package to Baku, along with updated mirror and halo profiling aimed at improving downstream airflow.

The upgrades appeared to pay off on a circuit that has traditionally suited Red Bull's low-drag philosophy, with its long main straight and 90-degree corners rewarding traction over high-speed cornering performance.

But Verstappen was cautious about reading too much into the result, pointing out that Baku's characteristics do not necessarily reflect what lies ahead on the calendar.

"I think also the parts that we got on the car in Baku, they worked well," he said.

"But we also know that Baku always has been quite a good track to us. It's quite unique with the 90-degree corners.

"You don't really have a lot of high-speed corners, so we have to wait a little bit now in the coming races [to see] how our car is going to perform, which is also quite good for us probably, to see all these different kinds of tracks.

"For next year, we'll probably learn a lot now over these coming races of what we need, what we want to do with the car.

"We're anyway not fighting for the championship, so for us it's a big learning curve. But, of course, the last few weekends have been a lot better than the start of the season."

title: Fernando Alonso names 'hardest thing' in deciding to remain in F1
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has detailed the "hardest thing" he had to reckon with whilst making his decision over his future in F1.

Alonso, the two-time world champion, announced on Tuesday that he would be staying with Aston Martin for the 2027 season, his 24th in grand prix racing.

By the end of it, he could be on 472 grand prix starts, or 39.46% of every world championship grand prix run, and also become the first 46-year-old to compete since Maurice Trintignant at the 1964 French GP.

However, Alonso's decision to stay comes as he wrestled with the decision given his loathing of the current generation of cars, which he has claimed are not challenging to drive, and that the "chef" or even Aston Martin's press officer could drive, and that fast corners have been reduced to "charging stations" for the "battery world championship."

It was these push factors Alonso had to weigh up against the pull of staying in F1, as he explained.

"That's a good question because that was the hardest thing for me," Alonso said when asked by BBC Sport how he could square continuing on in a championship he currently doesn't enjoy.

"This year, there have been some good races and some bad races. Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving.

"And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that.

"Maybe even for next year they can tweak the battery power a little bit to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving.

"Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight goes against the driver's instinct of braking late and going on power earlier.

"It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you end up going slower and that's not the way it should be."

The article continues below.

Alonso as elder statesman

Alonso, who has competed in nearly 40% of every F1 world championship grand prix ever, and won 32 times, gained 106 podiums, and is one of four active world champions, believes that he has "some responsibility to help the sport" correct course.

"It does help that the sport keeps chasing ideas and talking to the drivers and the teams (about) how to make things better, even for the next set of regulations," he said.

"This gives me also some hope that I will enjoy the driving more next year than I did this year."

title: Lando Norris shies away from Franco Colapinto penalty debate after clear-the-air talks
excerpt:
Lando Norris has changed his tune in assessing the severity of Franco Colapinto's grid penalty for this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after the two drivers cleared the air in a phone call following his demand for a race ban.

Norris was eliminated from Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after Colapinto lost control of his Alpine at Turn 1 on a safety car restart, clattering into team-mate Pierre Gasly, who then collided with Norris.

Colapinto was initially handed a 10-second time penalty for the incident that was converted into a five-place grid drop for this weekend's race at the Sepang International Circuit.

In the immediate aftermath, Norris had called for the FIA to introduce tougher sanctions.

"If you cause a crash on a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban," the McLaren driver said. "I think the FIA should be more strict and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff.

"It's careless of people. It costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin now. So yeah, people should just get banned. That's not driving."

[Article continues below]

Norris - 'Not my decision'

But the 26-year-old has since apologised, both publicly on social media and directly to Colapinto by phone.

"It didn't need to be a long conversation," said Norris, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "It was just a hello.

"I apologised to him for the words and some of the things I said that were wrong, and he apologised to me for the incident and the crash, which is good.

"I like Franco a lot. He's a very nice guy. We always talk on our track walk, on our drivers' parades, and things like that, so I have a lot of time for him.

"We were both just apologising to each other, nothing more than that."

As to whether he now felt the five-place penalty was appropriate, Norris refused to be drawn.

"On the penalty, it is difficult to say," he said. "It's not my decision."

Colapinto confirmed the pair had spoken and moved on from the incident, adding that he understood why Norris reacted as he did in the heat of the moment.

title: Mercedes combat W17 weakness with rare F1 upgrade
excerpt:
Mercedes has delivered a rare upgrade to its car for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, which is targeted at remedying its most glaring and fundamental weakness, as explained by RacingNews365 technical analyst Paolo Filisetti.

Mercedes has arrived at the Sepang International Circuit with an extensive aerodynamic upgrade designed to boost the overall downforce generated by the body of the W17.

The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia marks the first significant update delivered by the Brackley-based squad since the round in Montreal, back in May.

The changes are most visible around the sidepod profile, which now features a straight ramp angled towards the rear of the car. The bodywork at the back of the sidepods now drops right down to kerb height in front of the rear wheels.

The new sidepod shape is also highlighted by the angle of the cockpit-level gills, though it is even more apparent in the specification built for the climates of Sepang and Singapore.

The gills positioned further back, at engine hood level, show just how radically the rear section has been slimmed down.

That specific bodywork angle is designed to guide the airflow towards the rear axle without letting it separate from the surface.

The floor has also been significantly reworked around the diffuser throat, altering the pressure distribution at the exit.

Check out the W17's upgraded sidepod below! Article continues after...

© RacingNews365

© RacingNews365

© RacingNews365

Downforce gain without a drag penalty

The combined effect of the new sidepod profile, which conceals a completely revised internal airflow, and the updated floor is understood to produce a notable increase in downforce, in the region of almost four per cent, without any corresponding rise in drag.

As outlined in the preview of these changes, the update does not overhaul the aerodynamic concept of the W17 but rather sharpens it in terms of outright performance.

It is expected to improve the car's dynamic balance in sections of track where the W17 has so far lacked downforce and traction, namely on the exit of slow corners — one of the few genuine weak points of a car that owes much of its success not only to the strength of its power unit but also to its overall balance.

Sepang, with its two long straights and sequences of fast corners, appears to be the ideal venue to put that development to the test, one that Mercedes engineers are understood to have targeted from the car's early design phase.

title: Charles Leclerc lashes out at 'disrespectful' Fred Vasseur rumours in Christian Horner storm
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has lashed out at what he has called "disrespectful" rumours linking Christian Horner with taking Fred Vasseur's job at Ferrari.

Over the Azerbaijan GP weekend, Horner claimed in an interview with The Times that Ferrari was the "dream job" and the only team he would consider joining in F1 as not part of the ownership structure and merely an employee, as he was at Red Bull before his dismissal in 2025.

Addressing those claims for the first time in Baku, Vasseur, the current Ferrari team principal, felt that the "serenity" of Ferrari had been disrupted by Horner's effective 'Come and get me' plea.

Between the Azerbaijan and Bahrain GP in Malaysia races, Ferrari then organised a surprise media briefing where it was made clear that chairman John Elkann and CEO Benedetto Vigna enjoyed "full confidence" in Vasseur, who has been at the helm since replacing Mattia Binotto ahead of the 2023 season.

Speaking for the first time himself, Leclerc believes that the ongoing rumours of Horner to Ferrari is "disrespectful" to Vasseur.

"I've always said how much I trust Fred and how important he is for the team, he is extremely capable in what he does, and I think he's been extremely valuable so far, and he will be extremely valuable in the years to come as well," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"There was never any doubt inside the team that he has all our of support - and sometimes, it's needed to make it clear to the outside world as well, but to me, that doesn't matter as I know where we stand inside the team - and that's the most important.

"I just wish that there were fewer of these silly rumours going around.

"By definition, I think if you don't spend time speaking about the right things at the factory and pushing in the same direction, if you have these kinds of rumours, you spend maybe a bit more time speaking about these kinds of things, which is not nice, and how much of an effect it has, I don't think it is black and white.

"It's a bit more difficult to weigh in the effects that it has, but I don't think it does any good, that's for sure. Honestly, it's just not nice to see these kind of things. We are trying to do our best. Fred and all of us in the team, we are pushing ourselves to the limit.

"I find it a little bit disrespectful to see so many rumours. It is a part of our job to take criticism, but when you spread these kinds of things over and over, I think, at one point, it is just not so respectful."

The article continues below.

Leclerc back Ferrari 'serenity'

Leclerc was also questioned about Vasseur's comment from Azerbaijan, in which he claimed the "serenity" of Ferrari was being disrupted - something he agreed with.

"I don't see much of what is going around, but of course, you hear about what is going around and many people from the team know what is going around," he said.

"That is not good for the serenity of the team, but at the end of the day, this is something we have little control over, and we've got to maximise our results.

"[Vasseur's] strength is to manage people, and I think it is where you've got to be good when you are a team principal.

"He knows what words to use and what conditions are needed for someone to extract the maximum from the individual, and that is why he is so important for the team."

title: Isack Hadjar outlines repeat Red Bull plan after 'huge step'
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar will approach the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in a similar way to his stellar weekend in Baku — but for a very different reason.

Isack Hadjar plans to build up through the weekend at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in the same way he did on his return to the RB22 cockpit in Azerbaijan, after Red Bull's late-season upgrade delivered what he called a "huge step" in Baku.

The Frenchman missed three consecutive rounds, at Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid, after fracturing the outer side of his left wrist during a training session over the F1 summer break.

Rather than opting for surgery, Hadjar and Red Bull allowed the injury to heal naturally, with the team keeping him out until he was entirely free of pain.

Liam Lawson deputised for him across all three events, with Yuki Tsunoda in turn covering Lawson's seat at Racing Bulls.

Hadjar's return in Baku coincided with what Red Bull management described as the team's final major aerodynamic upgrade of the season, featuring revisions to the floor body, diffuser and sidepods.

The Milton Keynes-based squad has since redirected the bulk of its engineering resources towards its 2027 project, making the Baku package effectively the last significant update the RB22 will receive this year.

The result was a double podium in Azerbaijan, with Max Verstappen second and Hadjar third, his second podium finish of the season and the team's first result of that nature since early 2024.

'Step by step' again in Sepang

Hadjar said the outcome in Baku had exceeded expectations given the circumstances of his comeback.

"Baku was a really positive weekend for us," the three-time F1 podium finisher said ahead of the round at the Sepang International Circuit.

"Coming back after missing three races and scoring my second podium with the team was a great feeling, and having both cars on the podium was a huge step for everyone."

Hadjar is again planning for a gradual approach to the weekend, which in Baku was dictated by his lack of recent mileage after injury. In Malaysia, however, it stems from unfamiliarity with a circuit he has never raced on.

"Sepang looks like a really cool circuit, but it's my first time racing there, so the focus is just to build up through the weekend and take it step by step like we did in Baku," he added.

"The upgrades worked well there, which was positive, but Sepang has a different track layout, so we'll have to see where we stand."

title: Haas launch strong Esteban Ocon defence despite wielding axe
excerpt:
Haas boss Ayao Komatsu has launched a strong defence of Esteban Ocon - despite deciding to drop the Frenchman from the team for 2027.

Ocon announced on Wednesday that he would be departing Haas at the end of the current season after a two-year stay with the team - and vowed that it would not signal the end of his grand prix career.

However, Ocon will not be on the 2027 grid in a full-time race seat as the only seats remaining are those at Haas, which has just dropped him, at Mercedes and Racing Bulls, the latter of which is already facing its own driver conundrum with three drivers fighting over two seats in incumbents Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, with F2 title contender Nikola Tsolov hopeful of a promotion to F1.

A return for 2028 is possible, with Ocon declaring that he "deserves" to be on the grid when speaking to the media ahead of the Bahrain GP.

When his team boss was then questioned publicly for the first time since the announcement was made, Komatsu strongly defended Ocon.

"When we look at the overall picture, I think for me, it was time to make a change, but in terms of his ultimate speed and the performance he can produce when everything lines up, there is no doubt," Komatsu told media, including RacingNews365.

"I don't want to get dragged into specifics, and all I am saying is that the speed is there and he has shown he can perform at the highest level. That's what I am focusing on in the next races.

"Because if I say certain things, I'm sure you pick up on particular bits and take it out of context and write whatever you want, so I am not letting that happen because our best interest is for the team to provide the best environment for Esteban for the rest of the season, and for Esteban to be absolutely 100% focused on every single race to perform. That is what is best for the team.

"That is what is best for Esteban Ocon. He needs to show the world how fast he is, and as he showed in Baku, he is a great team player when we needed him to back off a little bit so that Oliver could have overtake mode because he was under pressure from [Arvid] Lindblad.

"He did it straight away, and he asked: 'Is that enough?' and I said: 'Yeah, that was good enough,' so he got to show the world his speed, and even though we just announced that he is leaving the team, he can be a team player.

"That's the best thing for Esteban Ocon, so I am not going to give you guys a chance to write anything other than that to distract him."

The article continues below.

Haas defend Ocon

Speaking about his decision to chase Ocon after his departure from Alpine in 2024, Komatsu felt the Frenchman had brought the race-winning nouse the team required - being the only grand prix winner to drive for the team.

"He brought the experience, and was the first driver signed who was a race winner," Komatsu said.

"He brought that experience, that dimension we didn't have as a team and then the combination of having Esteban with 10 years' experience and a race-winner, a proven-finisher with an exciting new talent in Oliver Bearman.

"He's not looking anymore like the rookie, and that was a very good combination, so I'm happy we signed Esteban a year-and-a-half ago, and we've had a good year-and-a-half.

"Honestly, the focus is on the eight races to go and to finish on a high.

"I think he deserves that, and the team deserves that, and I'm sure if we are focused on it without any other noise, we can achieve that."
